text.p: Stocks are expected to struggle this week, with action in the dollar and congressional testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan keeping Wall Street off balance.

The once-mighty technology stocks are also expected to see further selling pressure as money rotates into other groups, including shares of consumer non-durable companies, which promise more stable earnings, analysts said.

"Things have changed," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment strategist at First Albany Corp. "There is less urgency on the part of portfolio managers to put the flow of cash going into mutual funds and pension funds to work right away."
The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 4.24 points at 6,931.62 on Friday. But the index finshed down 57.34 points for the week.

Analysts said investors this week will focus on the dollar, which has pulled back from its sharp gains against foreign currencies in recent weeks. A further retreat by the dollar could lead foreign investors to turn away from U.S. financial markets, they said.

"There are genuine worries that the dollar has peaked and that we will see it decline, perhaps through the coordinated efforts of central banks, and that will cause some foreign investors to shy away from our bond market," Johnson said.
He said foreigners owned over 20 percent of U.S. Treasury bonds and account for 20 percent of daily activity.

Michael Metz, chief investment officer at Oppenheimer Co., who describes himself as a long-time bear and "a man who is extraordinarily uneasy and concerned about the near-term outlook for financial markets," is even more dire in his call.
Metz said the dollar had made at least a temporary peak and that the huge flow of capital into U.S. markets would "slow or end."

"The implication is that you will have the unwinding of huge speculative positions in the U.S. bond market which will cause a big move up in interest rates," he said. "That will dramatise the overvaluation of the American stock market and terminate the rush of foreign money into U.S. equities."

Federal Reserve Chairman Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony Wednesday and Thursday will also give investors pause. When it comes to Greenspan, Wall Street is always wary, doubting he will say anything to spark a rally but fearing he may give investors an excuse to sell, analysts said.
"'No harm' is what everyone wants from Greenspan," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities.
High-technology stocks will remain out of favour during the week, analysts said.

"Investors have gone from buying on very dip to lightening positions on every rally," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josepthal Lyon & Ross. "It's not that they don't like the high-technology stocks, but they own so many that just want to own less."
He said he expected investors to rotate into stocks of companies producing consumer non-durable goods, with their promise of more consistent earnings.
"You have great companies at prices that are lousy for investors," Blumberg said.
"They would rather own Procter & Gamble or Gillette than pay record multiples for International Business Machines and Intel Corp.," he added.
Economic data this week include February consumer confidence on Tuesday, January durable goods on Thursday and the fourth-quarter revised gross domestic product on Friday.
